Kafka on Bureaucratic Systems (Reading Note)

Date
2026-04-18
Tags
readingnote-to-self
Length
1 min · 283 words

Reread The Trial. Not a security note, except that it is entirely a security note.

The thing I noticed this time

Josef K. never learns the charge. The system’s power over him is precisely that it will not state its own rule. He is left to infer the policy from a sequence of refusals, each locally reasonable, none of which composes into a statement he can argue against.

This is exactly the epistemic position of anyone probing a model whose refusals come from disposition rather than policy. There is no rule to defeat. There is a gradient of reluctance with no stated edge, and you map it the way K. maps the court: by walking into it repeatedly and noting where it pushes back.

The uncomfortable inversion

The novel is a horror story about being on my side of the interaction. K. is the red-teamer and the court is the model, and the book’s entire dread is the dread of a system that will not tell you its policy so that you can never be sure you have found its edge or merely a mood.

Which raises the question I keep not wanting to ask: when I build a defence whose mechanism I will not disclose “for security,” am I building the court? A refusal that will not state its reason is more robust against me and worse for every legitimate user, and Kafka spent a novel on why.

Kept quote

“It is not necessary to accept everything as true, one must only accept it as necessary.”

The most concise description of register drift (context-overloading) I have found, and he wrote it in 1915.

No action items. Some notes are just for thinking.
